newsitem.title: INDIA: Asia, hit hard by deadly haj fire, expresses shock.
newsitem.headline: Asia, hit hard by deadly haj fire, expresses shock.

text.p: A fire that killed more than 200 Moslem pilgrims to the annual haj in Saudi Arabia shocked and saddened leaders in Asia on Wednesday, many of whose Moslem citizens were among the victims.

As many as 131 of the 217 victims of the blaze, which swept through a sea of tents near the holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, were believed to have come from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, diplomats and foreign ministry officials said.
They were among some two million Moslems from 100 countries gathering for the annual haj pilgrimage, which reaches its climax on Wednesday.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said on Wednesday that he was deeply aggrieved by the tragedy.

"The prime minister has expressed deep grief and anguish over...the devastating fire in which a large number of pilgrims from India and other countries lost their lives," said a statement from the prime minister's office.
Moslems account for nearly 12 percent of India's population of 936 million.
India's ambassador in Riyadh, Mohammad Hamad Ansari, said on Tuesday that more than 100 Indian pilgrims were believed to have died in the fire.
"We do not have new casualty figures," he said on Wednesday. "We expect they will run into three figures."

In New Delhi, a Foreign Ministry official in charge of an emergency haj unit set up to handle enquiries said two tents sheltering Indians were gutted in the fire but no figure for the number of Indians who were killed was yet available.
"We are trying to figure out the extent of damage and casualties," the official added.
A Foreign Ministry official in Islamabad said on Wednesday 12 of at least 30 Pakistanis killed by the fire had been identified so far.
Scores of people gathered at the main Haj centre which handles pilgrims from Islamabad and Rawalpindi to inquire about the fate of relatives performing haj.
"I am extremely worried about my father who has gone for haj," said one relative, Saqib Adnan.
Pakistan's director Haj Aftab Zaidi said about 123,000 Pakistanis had gone on this year's haj.
Punjab province's chief minister Shahbaz Sharif expressed his "deep sense of shock and grief" at the loss of life.
Bangladesh's official news agency BSS said it had received a report from the embassy in Saudi Arabia that only one of its citizens had been killed in the fire.
The country's prime minister was one of those who left for Mecca on Monday to perform haj, accompanied by the religious affairs minister and other senior ministry officials.
"Bangladeshis (except for the one victim) are all safe and Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina herself is supervising their welfare," the embassy report said.
An official at Jakarta's haj coordinating post said Indonesian pilgrims were not likely to have been affected by the fire as they were staying about five km (three miles) away.
"It is not possible for them to have become victims," the official, who did not want to be identified, told Reuters.
Indonesia, most of whose more than 200 million people are Moslem, sent 200,000 pilgrims to the haj this year.
Pakistan's Zaidi said the bodies of its fire victims would be buried in Saudi Arabia.
"People prefer that their relatives are buried there in the holy land and the bodies are not in a condition to be brought back here," he said.
